title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
TipTL;DR



Over three days I took an old Dell laptop, installed Fedora Server, made it reachable from anywhere over Tailscale despite being on locked-down campus Wi-Fi, and deployed a small team of AI agents on it. Every morning and evening it emails me a briefing with my calendar and to-dos. Every night it sorts my inbox into labels, and twice a day it sends me a report on what came in. Checkboxes I write in my Obsidian notes become Trello cards within seconds and get filed as done when I tick them, and I can chat with the whole system from Discord or Telegram on my phone or PC. It costs at most $15 a month, and that limit is enforced, not hoped for.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
2.1 Laptop or cloud?
Before committing, I considered just renting a droplet instead. The laptop won:









Old laptop
Cloud VM with 8 GB RAM




Cost
A few dollars of electricity
Roughly $10–48/month depending on provider


Where my credentials live
At home
On someone else’s machine


Public exposure
None needed
Usually a public IP


Survives power cuts / outages
No
Yes



Because everything lives under one folder and is backed up with restic, moving to the cloud later is a restore, not a rebuild. So I started on the laptop, and I’ll only move if outages actually start to bother me.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
3.1 Fedora Server 44, fresh
The laptop was running Fedora 40, which had already stopped getting security updates. Rather than upgrade in place, I wiped it and installed Fedora Server 44. Going without a desktop frees up roughly another gigabyte of RAM for the agents, and SSH, Cockpit (a web admin panel) and the firewall all come preconfigured. In the installer I ticked Headless Management (Cockpit), Container Management (Podman) and Hardware Support (for the Wi-Fi drivers). I did consider Debian 13 for its roughly five-year support window, but I know Fedora, and one upgrade a year is a price I’m willing to pay for that.






WarningTwo installer gotchas



Fedora Server gives / only 15 GB by default, even on a 256 GB disk. You can either choose custom storage in the installer or grow it afterwards:
sudo lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/mapper/fedora-root
df -h /     # should now show ~237 GB
Server editions also may not ship Wi-Fi support. My Ethernet was down, so my fallback was USB tethering from my phone, then:
sudo dnf install NetworkManager-wifi iwlwifi-mvm-firmware
sudo nmcli device wifi connect "MyNetwork" password "..."
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
section: 3.2 Lid closed, never sleeping, screen off
text:
3.2 Lid closed, never sleeping, screen off
A laptop wants to sleep when you close it. A server must not. I used a drop-in config (edited with vim) to ignore the lid, then masked every sleep target:


/etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/server.conf

[Login]
HandleLidSwitch=ignore
HandleLidSwitchExternalPower=ignore
HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore

sudo systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target hybrid-sleep.target
sudo reboot
systemctl status sleep.target     # "masked" and "dead" is exactly what you want
To keep the screen from burning out its backlight on a shelf, I blank the console after five minutes, run a small boot service that turns the backlight off entirely, and set up a toggle key (or the laptop’s own brightness keys) for the rare times I need the physical console:
sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="consoleblank=300"
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
3.3 Automatic updates
dnf5-automatic installs security updates on a timer. The first failure I saw was a Could not resolve host at 06:08, which turned out to be a momentary campus Wi-Fi drop rather than a broken config. If it keeps happening, my plan is to turn off Wi-Fi power saving and let the update service retry on its own:


systemctl edit dnf5-automatic.service

[Service]
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10min
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
4.1 Tailscale
Tailscale solves all three problems. Every device makes an outgoing connection to the Tailscale coordination service and gets a stable private address and name on my own private network (a “tailnet”), so I can SSH to the server by name from my dorm, from class, or from my phone on mobile data.
curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh
sudo tailscale up --qr          # prints a QR code: scan it with your phone to sign in
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-interface=tailscale0
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Two details are easy to miss. The --qr flag is the trick for a machine with no browser, since you sign in by scanning the code with your phone. And you’ll want to disable key expiry for the server in the Tailscale admin page, or it quietly logs itself out after 180 days. To confirm a session really came in over Tailscale, check the source address:
echo $SSH_CONNECTION     # first address starting with 100. means it's the tailnet
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
4.2 Closing the front door
Once SSH over Tailscale worked, I removed SSH and Cockpit from the campus-facing firewall zone. The server is now invisible to the dorm network, and only my own devices can even reach a login prompt:
ZONE=$(sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone)
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=$ZONE --remove-service=ssh
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=$ZONE --remove-service=cockpit
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
SSH keys are the second lock. Cockpit is still available in a browser on port 9090, but only over the tailnet.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
4.3 Backups
Backups go to a USB stick with restic every night at 03:00, keeping 14 daily, 8 weekly and 12 monthly snapshots. Fedora Server doesn’t auto-mount USB drives, so the stick gets a permanent mount point with nofail, which means the machine still boots if the stick is unplugged:


/etc/fstab (one added line)

UUID=XXXX-XXXX  /mnt/backup  exfat  uid=1000,gid=1000,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=5s  0 0







NoteSide quest: reformatting the installer stick





The USB stick was still laid out as a Fedora installer, which Windows can’t read. After wipefs and a new GPT partition table, mkfs.exfat still refused with “Device has existing signatures”: the new partition started at the same offset as the old one, so the old FAT32 label was still inside it. One more sudo wipefs -a /dev/sdX1 on the partition fixed it.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
section: 5.1 Two harnesses, one set of tools
text:
5.1 Two harnesses, one set of tools
The key design decision was to make every integration an MCP server and have both harnesses load the same servers. An agent is then just a prompt, a tool allowlist and a schedule, and I can run it in either harness without building anything twice.





flowchart TB
    phone["Phone / PC<br/>Discord, Telegram"]
    notes["Obsidian on phone and PC"]
    hermes["Hermes Agent<br/>chat, memory, ad-hoc requests"]
    sdk["Claude Agent SDK workers<br/>secretary, email, underwriter, drive<br/>on systemd timers"]
    code["Plain-code jobs<br/>briefings, vault watcher, backups"]
    subgraph tools["Shared MCP tool servers"]
      google["google<br/>Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Sheets, Slides"]
      trello["trello<br/>lists, cards, checklists"]
      team["team<br/>hand-offs between agents"]
    end
    vault[("Obsidian vault<br/>git history")]
    phone --> hermes
    hermes --> tools
    sdk --> tools
    code --> trello
    code --> google
    notes <-->|Syncthing| vault
    vault --> code


 Architecture: two harnesses share one set of MCP tool servers. 



My rule of thumb for dividing the work is simple: anything scheduled and risky goes to an SDK worker, anything conversational and exploratory goes to Hermes, and anything that’s always the same steps is just plain code.









Claude Agent SDK
Hermes Agent




Role
Scheduled jobs that must not misbehave
Chat front door from my phone


Strength
Hard tool allowlist, per-run dollar cap, code-level hooks
Messaging gateway, memory, skills, cron, profiles


Runs as
systemd --user timers
A long-lived gateway service


Model
Picked per job
Haiku (cheap) in hybrid mode
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
5.2 Hand-offs as plain files
Agents pass work to each other through the team MCP server, which is deliberately boring: one JSON file per hand-off in a new/ folder, moved to done/ with a result. It works from either harness, survives restarts, and I can debug it with ls.





sequenceDiagram
    participant Me as Me (phone)
    participant Vault as Obsidian vault
    participant U as Underwriter
    participant Q as team hand-off queue
    participant S as Secretary
    participant T as Trello
    Me->>Vault: "- [ ] Renew registration due 11/1"
    Vault->>U: note syncs to server
    U->>Q: send_handoff(to=secretary, add_todo)
    S->>Q: picks up hand-off
    S->>T: creates card with checklist and due date
    S->>Q: completes hand-off with card link

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
6.1 A model per job
Not every job needs the same amount of judgment, so each job picks its own model tier:


agents/models.py (excerpt)

JOBS = {
    "secretary.handoffs": ("haiku", "low"),      # turn queued to-dos into Trello cards
    "secretary.morning": ("sonnet", "medium"),   # briefing email + booking focus blocks
    "secretary.ask": ("sonnet", "medium"),       # "book the dentist Tuesday at 3"
    "underwriter": ("haiku", "low"),             # tags, links, to-do extraction from notes
    "email.triage": ("haiku", "low"),            # nightly: label, archive, flag junk
    "email.report": ("sonnet", "medium"),        # morning/night report emails
    "email.draft": ("sonnet", "medium"),         # drafts to people you name
    "drive": ("opus", "high"),                   # Slides decks, Sheets, Colab notebooks
}

RUN_CAP_USD = {"haiku": 0.25, "sonnet": 0.75, "opus": 3.00}

Any job can be overridden from the environment file (MODEL_EMAIL_TRIAGE=sonnet) without touching code.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
6.2 Three setups
I built three separate, fully documented ways to run the same codebase, so I could choose based on cost.

Budget ($0)Hybrid (≤ $15/month), what I runFull Claude (~$30–75/month)


The budget setup uses no API key at all. Plain Python sends the briefing emails and syncs Obsidian checkboxes to Trello, and an optional small local model (Qwen3 4B via Ollama) tags notes overnight. There’s no chat bot, because Hermes needs far more context than this laptop can serve locally.


Hybrid includes everything in Budget for free, then adds Claude Haiku for the phone chat bot, the nightly inbox sorting and the twice-daily inbox reports, and Claude Sonnet for one-off requests and email drafts. There’s a hard cap of $15/month in the Anthropic Console, plus a $5/month sub-budget for the scheduled agents so they can’t eat into the chat budget. I estimate typical spend at about $2–6/month.


In the full setup, Claude writes the briefings and books focus blocks itself, an underwriter agent understands free-form notes instead of fixed checkbox syntax, and Opus builds decks and spreadsheets. I estimate $30–75/month, mostly from chat and email. All-Opus would be $80–180.









ImportantThese are estimates



The cost figures come from typical token counts (a run reads ~100k tokens, much of it cached, and writes ~4k), not from measurements. The real numbers will come from the Console’s usage page after a few weeks of running.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
6.3 One command to switch
The difference between hybrid and full is more than “Haiku vs Sonnet”. It also changes which timers run, so I never get both the free and the Claude-written morning email, and it changes the spending caps. So I made it one command:
$ agent-mode hybrid
✓ agent-team.env: hybrid settings (previous copy saved as agent-team.env.bak)
✓ Hermes chat model: claude-haiku-5-5
✓ Hermes restarted
✓ timers on: briefing-morning, briefing-evening, vault-watch, vault-commit, email-triage, backup, ...
✓ timers off: secretary-morning, secretary-evening, secretary-handoffs, ...
agent-mode full flips it back, and agent-mode status shows the mode, the timers and the month’s spend. The bot can also answer “what have I spent this month?” through a small spend_this_month tool.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
7.1 Accounts and secrets
I needed three accounts: an Anthropic API key (with a spend limit), a Google Cloud OAuth client, and a Trello API key and token.
All of the secrets live in one file outside the repo, readable only by my user. The folder is chmod 700 (folders need the execute bit to be entered) and the file is chmod 600. The server pulls code with a read-only deploy key scoped to that one repository rather than a key on my GitHub account, so if the laptop is ever compromised, nothing else is exposed. For the proof of concept I’m using a throwaway Gmail account as a sandbox; switching to my real account later is a config change and one sign-in.






NoteTwo account-setup surprises





Trello only issues API keys through a “Power-Up”, even if you never build one, and the form demands an iframe URL that’s never used. Any https address works.
You should also publish the Google OAuth app. It stays unverified and private to you, but in “testing” mode Google signs the agents out every 7 days.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
section: 8.1 Checkboxes become Trello cards in seconds
text:
8.1 Checkboxes become Trello cards in seconds
This is the feature I use most, and it involves no AI at all. I write a line in any note, on any device:
- [ ] Pay rent #home due 11/1
    - [ ] transfer from savings
    - [ ] send receipt to roommate
About five seconds after the note syncs, a small watcher service on the server notices the change. It picks the Trello list from the first #tag that matches a list name, creates a card with the sub-items as a checklist and the due date set to 09:00, and writes a [Trello](...) link back into the line so it’s never sent twice. When I tick the box, the card moves to Done. If a sync race strips the link before I tick it, the script finds the card it made for that line and relinks it.


vault-watch.service (excerpt)

[Service]
ExecStart=%h/server/apps/agent-team/.venv/bin/python scripts/vault_watch.py
Restart=always
RestartSec=30
Nice=10







WarningThe mystery of the 2 GB vault



My nightly backup suddenly took minutes instead of seconds. The vault, which held seven tiny notes (~1.5 KB according to Syncthing), was 2 GB on disk.
The culprit: I had briefly pointed Syncthing at a PC folder containing two large videos, then deleted them mid-transfer. Syncthing left its hidden, half-finished .syncthing.*.tmp files behind. Syncthing doesn’t count those, but the hourly git snapshot happily committed them. Deleting .git alone didn’t help, because the very next commit saved them again.
The fix was to remove the temp files, start a fresh history, and permanently ignore Syncthing’s partial downloads:
rm -f ./.syncthing.*.tmp
printf '%s\n' '.syncthing.*.tmp' '~syncthing~*.tmp' >> .gitignore
After that, restic unlock and restic prune reclaimed the space on the backup drive. The ignore rule is now part of my setup steps.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
9.1 Setting it up safely
The setup wizard has a lot of options, and the defaults are generous. Here’s what I chose:








Wizard screen
Choice
Why




Setup mode
Full setup (bring your own key)
“Quick setup” uses a different model provider and would bypass my Anthropic key and its $15 cap


Terminal backend
Docker/Podman
If the bot is ever tricked into running a command, it runs in a container that can’t touch my files or secrets


Egress firewall
On
A tricked command can’t send data anywhere; the real tools run outside the container


Toolsets
Only Skills, Memory, Session Search, Clarifying Questions, Task Planning
Every enabled tool’s description is sent with every message, so each one costs tokens; several also add risk


Platforms
None in the wizard
Added later with hermes gateway setup



Then I merged my MCP servers into Hermes’s config, so it gets the same Trello, Google and team tools as the SDK workers:


~/.hermes/config.yaml (excerpt)

model:
  provider: "anthropic"
  default: "claude-haiku-5-5"   # set by `agent-mode hybrid`

mcp_servers:
  trello:
    command: ".../.venv/bin/python"
    args: [".../mcp_servers/trello_server.py"]
  google:
    command: "uvx"
    args: ["workspace-mcp", "--single-user", "--tools", "calendar", "gmail", "drive", "sheets", "slides"]
    tools:
      exclude: ["send_gmail_message", "manage_gmail_filter", "*delete*"]







NoteThe bot that blamed Trello



After I connected Discord, the bot started running shell commands and then claimed “Trello is rate-limited.” Two separate things were going on.
First, each chat platform has its own toolset list. I had trimmed tools only for the CLI, so Discord and Telegram kept the defaults, terminal included. The egress firewall blocked every command, so the safety net worked, but the real fix was to trim those lists too.
Second, the rate limit was invented. The vault watcher’s logs showed zero errors and no 429s. The model had made up a plausible explanation for its own failing terminal calls. When an agent explains a failure, check the logs before believing the explanation.
crumbs: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server

title: Haswell Meets Haiku - Using Antiquated Technology to Build a Personal Productivity Server
text:
9.2 Chatting from anywhere
The same Hermes instance answers on Discord (a private server with just me and the bot) and Telegram (a bot from @BotFather), on my iPhone and on my Windows PC, and allowed users are restricted to my own account IDs. I can ask “what’s due this week?”, “book the dentist Tuesday at 3”, “file my done cards” or “what have I spent this month?”. I also like Hermes’s terminal UI, so a Windows Terminal profile that opens it over Tailscale SSH is on my list.

title: APL Drone Development
text:
I worked at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory from June 10 to June 27. While there, I developed a quadcopter-style drone that demonstrated the ability for both autonomous and manual control from a Steam Deck controller. I established the data pathway between the Raspberry Pi and the Steam Deck, including the ability to use the joysticks in place of a radio controller to pilot the drone.
In addition to the drone’s development, I was able to experiment with using Asahi Linux on an Apple Silicon MacBook Pro, as well as begin reverse engineering the ArduPilot firmware for the Beelink F504 board. I feel that the reverse engineering presents a viable future for research, and I would like to continue studying the platform to better understand its vulnerabilities and function.



I built an autonomous quadcopter-style drone with what I would refer to as a “spread X” shaped frame and four 2306 1755KV motors, making the drone in the 5-6 inch size range. The size metric refers to the propeller size, not the actual drone size itself.
The physical components of the drone are as follows:

FC Stack: RADIX2HD
Computer: Raspberry Pi 4
Battery: CHNL 2200mAh 70C 7.4V Battery
Motors: Flight XING2 2306 1755KV Drone Motor
Camera: VIA Labs Camera




Upon assembly, I realized that the drone kit was missing several key components, first of which was the battery. I then performed research on the capabilities of the motors provided by the kit, and ordered the largest battery that I could find that provided the required voltage for the drone’s FC stack and motors. The large battery size provided additional range and ensured that the Raspberry Pi could be powered by the same battery as the FC stack assembly.



Top view of fully constructed drone


Next, I began tackling the communication problems. The documentation provided with the kit offered little to no actual documentation of how communication between devices and hardware would actually work, so I began researching and finally settled on QGroundControl as the flight software I would use on the computer itself. Before QGroundControl was useful, though, I needed to figure out how to connect the Raspberry Pi to the FC stack, and then the Pi to my computer where QGroundControl itself was running.
When I got the Raspberry Pi, I was unable to get it to connect to the JHU network, so I began by getting the Pi connected to a monitor and setting up some of its local settings. Upon logging into the Pi for the first time, I had my first glimpse at some software produced by whoever had been working on the drone before me. It seemed like a Python-based, homemade attempt at QGroundControl. I connected the Pi to the JHU-Visitor network and then enabled SSH on the Pi so that I could connect to it from my development machine.
After SSHing into the Pi, I used the command lsusb to determine the FC stack to be a RADIX2HD board running a version of ArduPilot as its firmware. I then spent time working with and reading the code for the GUI that was developed on the Raspberry Pi, and trying to get the drone to pass the pre-arm checks associated with arming from the Python script. However, I continually ran into the same issues with the ArduPilot firmware itself, which stopped me from being able to arm the drone with the home-built Python script.
After several hours of manipulating the Python script, I researched the firmware more and found the mavproxy.py command, which I then installed onto the Pi. This allowed me to run mavproxy.py, which would immediately connect the Pi to the FC stack and allowed me to change variables in the firmware, fixing the pre-arm check errors. However, the home-built software was still not playing nicely with the stack or the MAVProxy protocol. So I scrapped it and began using QGroundControl full time instead, as it was a more robust and industry-developed option.
In order to get QGroundControl to see the drone, I needed to route the MAVLink packets into one of the ports that QGroundControl looked at for connections. This led me to use the UDP protocol on port 14550, which I was able to accomplish by specifying the drone as a device and then using several flags in addition to the mavproxy.py command on my computer. This then allowed me to open the QGroundControl window and connect immediately to the drone.



The RADIX2FC flight stack. The SD card is where the firmware modules are flashed.


The flight stack of the drone uses ArduPilot to connect to the Raspberry Pi for autonomous flight. The Raspberry Pi gives the drone the potential to connect to my computer running QGroundControl and facilitate waypoint-based flight. The Pi also allows for an LLM to be installed onto it in order to allow for autonomous flight capabilities. It also has image recognition software that allows the drone to label and categorize images into larger categories.
I then needed to power the entire thing, Pi and all, from the same battery. Using a buck converter, I was able to assemble a wiring harness that allowed me to power the entire drone with the singular battery, despite the Pi needing a lower voltage than the FC stack. We did this by cutting an XT60 connector and splicing it into a smaller gauge wire, then running that into the converter. We then connected that to a USB-C stub cable and used it to power the Pi.



The wiring harness built for the drone. Joe Duva helped me design this and provided the buck converter that I used.





Until this point I had been connecting to and working with the drone entirely from my laptop running Ubuntu 24.04. However, included with the drone kit was a Steam Deck that seemed to be running Ubuntu. It was locked, and no one had the password, so I used the Ubuntu recovery menu to reset the password. I then began poking around to see if I could make the same processes work from the Steam Deck instead of the computer.
I quickly ran into several major roadblocks. For starters, using the apt command in any way resulted in an instant segmentation fault. Checking the package’s existence with dpkg was also confusing, as it listed the package as installed and existing. I got around this by downloading the .deb package from Ubuntu’s website and attempting to reinstall it with dpkg itself. This failed and gave me another set of errors, which required a different package. I downloaded that package and attempted to install it with dpkg, and got a different error that dpkg itself was corrupted. This led me to dig through the config files for dpkg itself, and realize that they had been completely corrupted.
After this revelation, I was able to recompile dpkg, and then build both of my required packages to get apt working again. Things went much quicker after that, and I was able to install and start the SSH service on the Deck, and then actually update the entire system to Ubuntu 22.04, which was required to run QGroundControl. I then was able to both SSH into the Pi from the Deck as well as pass back the MAVProxy packets to the Deck, allowing for connection to QGC on the Deck. I was close, but I couldn’t get the joysticks to work, which was the entire reason for using the Steam Deck: to bypass the need for a second controller or radio to fly the drone.



Steam Deck running QGroundControl


I began trying to get the joystick input drivers to work with QGC itself, but after a little while began to look for other options. Through some research, I realized that the Steam client could be used to run any program on the computer by loading it as a “non-Steam game.” This would allow the Steam client to import the Steam Deck’s controls into the application, as the client would run it in the same environment as it would run any video game. This gave me the ability to use the joysticks as the radio controls for the drone.



QGroundControl as a Steam game in my library


After getting the joysticks to work, I was able to pass all pre-flight checks aside from the GPS requirement, and actually execute a full launch sequence while the drone was taped down on the desk. It is very close to being completed.



In between getting cables and other physical supplies I needed for the drone, I was able to work on a few smaller projects. The first was installing Asahi Linux onto a 16-inch M1 Max MacBook Pro, which I did to test the distro as well as using Linux on the ARM-based processor. Asahi uses Fedora 42 as the kernel and GNOME as the stock window manager. Its limitations are that the MacBook Pro cannot use Thunderbolt or USB-C ports for additional displays, or run virtual machines, as the ARM-based architecture is not overly developed with Linux packages. While there may be a way to make QEMU or Virt-Manager work on the ARM-based Fedora install, I was unable to figure it out in the time I had before I was back to working on the drone. If VM support was available, it would greatly improve the usefulness of the MacBook Pro and make the device more worth its large price tag.



M1 Pro MacBook Pro running Fedora 42 with Sway and Alacritty


Secondly, I was able to take some of the Arduino ArduCopter firmware and begin reverse engineering it. I think that this area of vulnerability analysis would be an extremely fruitful area of research, and that better understanding the weaknesses with drone firmware could lead to breakthroughs in drone deterrence for both the private and military sectors.
As for the drone, next steps would include porting the camera into the QGroundControl application, as well as installing a GPS module and getting an antenna or radio to allow for communication without Wi-Fi. This would require some development on the Steam Deck as well, as I am unsure how that platform would work with a different antenna. A mesh network would also be interesting to investigate. I also would love to see what we could do with different scanners or radar on the actual drone, like a LiDAR scanner or infrared capabilities.



The drone uses the following communication stack:





flowchart TB
  pc["Ground Station<br/>(Steam Deck with QGroundControl)"]
  pi["Raspberry Pi<br/>(Onboard Computer)"]
  fc["Flight Controller<br/>(RADIX2HD)"]

  pc -->|"UDP / SSH via Wi-Fi<br/>port 14550"| pi
  pi -->|"UART / MAVLink<br/>/dev/ttyACM0"| fc
  fc -->|"Telemetry / Sensor Data"| pi
  pi -->|"Telemetry / MAVLink"| pc









SSH into the drone using the -X flag so that an X server is generated for the Raspberry Pi. The Raspberry Pi has its own drone control app that starts on login. Its only usage at this time is to operate the camera, and it does not succeed in arming the drone.
Exit the spawned window for controlling the drone.
Run the following command to connect to the drone via MAVProxy and forward the data back to the computer at port 14550, which is how the drone connects to QGroundControl:
mavproxy.py --master=/dev/<location_of_drone> \
  --baudrate 57600 \
  --out=udp:<pc_ip>:14550
Navigate to the Steam client. Open the client and go to your library.
Click the plus button and add the QGroundControl AppImage as a game.
Open the controller settings and make sure that it is being run with “Gamepad with Joystick Trackpad” mode enabled. Close the window.
Under settings, open properties/controller. Next to the “Override for QGC inputs” section, choose “Enable Steam Input” from the dropdown menu.
Run QGroundControl from the Steam launcher.
QGroundControl should automatically connect to the drone, as the packets are being forwarded at port 14550.




QGroundControl in the Steam Library with the MAVLink command prepared


Once QGroundControl is connected:

Inside QGC, enable centered joysticks for throttle control, and then check to see that the inputs are being mapped to QGC from the live menu.
Calibrate the radio inputs in the vehicle settings. Do not hold the throttle to the bottom of the bowl when shown. Allow the program to equalize with the stick in its resting position, and it will calibrate without issue.
Fly the drone.




Controller configuration. Calibration here before the radio is a good idea.





Calibrating the joysticks as the drone’s radio






I had a blast on this project and learned a great deal about drones, as well as ways that I could continue developing as both a computer scientist and an engineer. I had never been able to both build and code something before, and I found out that I loved it, as it brought together both my mechanical skill set and my CS abilities. I have found something I am passionate about and will be continuing to build devices, hopefully drones and other robots in the future.
I also learned a ton of Python from working on the MAVLink protocol, as well as a deeper understanding of communication and how signals can be passed over SSH to different programs. I used a great deal of my Linux knowledge and fixed a more complex problem than I had ever come across on the Steam Deck, which I really enjoyed as well. Finally, I found a huge category of things to reverse engineer, and will be looking deeper into drone firmware when I get time. I think that there is so much to see and exploit in cheap drone hardware, and I would love to spend more time actually exploring that area of cybersecurity and vulnerability research.

Will Gray-Roncall, who ordered me a ton of wiring, batteries, and everything else I needed, as well as allowed me to work on a drone in the first place. I am so glad he had it in the closet.
Blake, who got me the MacBook Pro from surplus and walked around with me to see the semiconductor foundries in building 13. Enjoy the Asahi MBP.

title: APL Drone Development
text:
I worked at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory from June 10 to June 27. While there, I developed a quadcopter-style drone that demonstrated the ability for both autonomous and manual control from a Steam Deck controller. I established the data pathway between the Raspberry Pi and the Steam Deck, including the ability to use the joysticks in place of a radio controller to pilot the drone.
In addition to the drone’s development, I was able to experiment with using Asahi Linux on an Apple Silicon MacBook Pro, as well as begin reverse engineering the ArduPilot firmware for the Beelink F504 board. I feel that the reverse engineering presents a viable future for research, and I would like to continue studying the platform to better understand its vulnerabilities and function.

title: APL Drone Development
text:
I built an autonomous quadcopter-style drone with what I would refer to as a “spread X” shaped frame and four 2306 1755KV motors, making the drone in the 5-6 inch size range. The size metric refers to the propeller size, not the actual drone size itself.
The physical components of the drone are as follows:

FC Stack: RADIX2HD
Computer: Raspberry Pi 4
Battery: CHNL 2200mAh 70C 7.4V Battery
Motors: Flight XING2 2306 1755KV Drone Motor
Camera: VIA Labs Camera

title: APL Drone Development
text:
Upon assembly, I realized that the drone kit was missing several key components, first of which was the battery. I then performed research on the capabilities of the motors provided by the kit, and ordered the largest battery that I could find that provided the required voltage for the drone’s FC stack and motors. The large battery size provided additional range and ensured that the Raspberry Pi could be powered by the same battery as the FC stack assembly.



Top view of fully constructed drone


Next, I began tackling the communication problems. The documentation provided with the kit offered little to no actual documentation of how communication between devices and hardware would actually work, so I began researching and finally settled on QGroundControl as the flight software I would use on the computer itself. Before QGroundControl was useful, though, I needed to figure out how to connect the Raspberry Pi to the FC stack, and then the Pi to my computer where QGroundControl itself was running.
When I got the Raspberry Pi, I was unable to get it to connect to the JHU network, so I began by getting the Pi connected to a monitor and setting up some of its local settings. Upon logging into the Pi for the first time, I had my first glimpse at some software produced by whoever had been working on the drone before me. It seemed like a Python-based, homemade attempt at QGroundControl. I connected the Pi to the JHU-Visitor network and then enabled SSH on the Pi so that I could connect to it from my development machine.
After SSHing into the Pi, I used the command lsusb to determine the FC stack to be a RADIX2HD board running a version of ArduPilot as its firmware. I then spent time working with and reading the code for the GUI that was developed on the Raspberry Pi, and trying to get the drone to pass the pre-arm checks associated with arming from the Python script. However, I continually ran into the same issues with the ArduPilot firmware itself, which stopped me from being able to arm the drone with the home-built Python script.
After several hours of manipulating the Python script, I researched the firmware more and found the mavproxy.py command, which I then installed onto the Pi. This allowed me to run mavproxy.py, which would immediately connect the Pi to the FC stack and allowed me to change variables in the firmware, fixing the pre-arm check errors. However, the home-built software was still not playing nicely with the stack or the MAVProxy protocol. So I scrapped it and began using QGroundControl full time instead, as it was a more robust and industry-developed option.
In order to get QGroundControl to see the drone, I needed to route the MAVLink packets into one of the ports that QGroundControl looked at for connections. This led me to use the UDP protocol on port 14550, which I was able to accomplish by specifying the drone as a device and then using several flags in addition to the mavproxy.py command on my computer. This then allowed me to open the QGroundControl window and connect immediately to the drone.



The RADIX2FC flight stack. The SD card is where the firmware modules are flashed.


The flight stack of the drone uses ArduPilot to connect to the Raspberry Pi for autonomous flight. The Raspberry Pi gives the drone the potential to connect to my computer running QGroundControl and facilitate waypoint-based flight. The Pi also allows for an LLM to be installed onto it in order to allow for autonomous flight capabilities. It also has image recognition software that allows the drone to label and categorize images into larger categories.
I then needed to power the entire thing, Pi and all, from the same battery. Using a buck converter, I was able to assemble a wiring harness that allowed me to power the entire drone with the singular battery, despite the Pi needing a lower voltage than the FC stack. We did this by cutting an XT60 connector and splicing it into a smaller gauge wire, then running that into the converter. We then connected that to a USB-C stub cable and used it to power the Pi.



The wiring harness built for the drone. Joe Duva helped me design this and provided the buck converter that I used.

title: Dotfiles
text:
Vim Plug is a minimalistic plugin manager that allows you to install plugins without creating an IDE out of Vim like LazyVim does.
vim-plug - Config (init.vim)
" tab -> 4 spaces
set tabstop=4
set shiftwidth=4
set expandtab

" numbers + syntax highlighting + line endings
set nu list
syntax on

autocmd FileType markdown syntax match markdownBold /\*\*\zs.*\ze\*\*/ containedin=ALL | highlight markdownBold ctermfg=Magenta guifg=#FF69B4

call plug#begin()

Plug 'tomasr/molokai'
Plug 'vim-airline/vim-airline'
Plug 'vim-airline/vim-airline-themes'
Plug 'lervag/vimtex'
Plug 'neanias/everforest-nvim', { 'branch': 'main' }
Plug 'maxmx03/fluoromachine.nvim', { 'branch': 'main'}
Plug 'loctvl842/monokai-pro.nvim'

call plug#end()

" theme
colorscheme monokai-pro-octagon
let g:rehash256 = 1

hi Normal ctermbg=none
hi NonText ctermbg=none
hi LineNr ctermbg=none

" vimtex
let g:vimtex_view_method = 'zathura'

" airline
let airline_theme='minimalist'

" air-line
let g:airline_powerline_fonts = 1

if !exists('g:airline_symbols')
    let g:airline_symbols = {}
endif

" unicode symbols
let g:airline_left_sep = '»'
let g:airline_left_sep = '▶'
let g:airline_right_sep = '«'
let g:airline_right_sep = '◀'
let g:airline_symbols.linenr = '␊'
let g:airline_symbols.linenr = '␤'
let g:airline_symbols.linenr = '¶'
let g:airline_symbols.branch = '⎇'
let g:airline_symbols.paste = 'ρ'
let g:airline_symbols.paste = 'Þ'
let g:airline_symbols.paste = '∥'
let g:airline_symbols.whitespace = 'Ξ'

" airline symbols
let g:airline_left_sep = ''
let g:airline_left_alt_sep = ''
let g:airline_right_sep = ''
let g:airline_right_alt_sep = ''
let g:airline_symbols.branch = ''
let g:airline_symbols.readonly = ''
let g:airline_symbols.linenr = ''

set omnifunc=htmlcomplete#CompleteTags
